turns.content: My parents have fixed a "meeting" this Sunday. A family from our community, the boy works in Dallas, my photo has apparently already been shared. What they don't know is I've been with someone for two years — a colleague. He's wonderful. He's also from a different caste, and in my house that word ends conversations. I have five days.

Five days. That's such a specific kind of dread — a countdown to something you never agreed to.

First, the thing I want you to hear: you haven't done anything wrong. Loving someone for two years isn't a betrayal of your family. But I understand why it feels like you're carrying a secret bomb into your own house.

Can I ask the real question underneath this? Is Sunday the deadline for *telling them about him* — or are you thinking of going through the meeting to buy time?

Because those are two very different paths. Sitting through the meeting might feel easier, but it deepens the tangle — the other family gets invested, your parents get hopeful, and your relationship stays hidden a little longer with higher stakes attached.

Telling them before Sunday is terrifying, yes. But you'd be telling them on *your* terms, not confessing after they've half-committed you to someone else. And you don't have to lead with caste. You can lead with: "There's someone. Two years. He's serious about me and I'm serious about him." Let them meet the fact of him before they meet the label.

What does he know about all this? Is he standing ready to face your family with you, or does he not know Sunday is happening?

And honestly — how do you *think* your parents will react? Anger that cools, or the kind that doesn't? That matters for how you plan this.

I tried hinting last month that I'm not ready and Amma's BP shot up the same evening, or at least that's what everyone told me it was. Appa has already mentioned Sunday to my uncle's family. It's not even about the Dallas guy — they're not bad people, that's the worst part. They're excited. They think this is them taking care of me.

That's the cruelest version of this, isn't it. If they were tyrants, you could be angry. Instead they're happy, they're planning, Amma is probably already thinking about what to serve — and every ounce of their love feels like a wall closing in.

But I want to gently name something: Amma's BP going up when you hinted, everyone making sure you knew about it — whether anyone intends it or not, that's how families teach daughters that their honesty is dangerous. That your truth is a health hazard. It works precisely because you're a loving person. And it will work at every stage — hinting, telling, engagement, wedding — unless you decide at some point that her BP can't be the thing that decides your life.

And Appa telling your uncle's family — that's the machinery starting. Each day, more people know, more face is at stake, and your eventual truth becomes a bigger "scandal" instead of a smaller conversation. Five days from now it's not just disappointing your parents; it's them "explaining" to relatives. That's why waiting rarely makes it gentler. It just raises the price.

Their excitement is real love. But love that hasn't been given the real information isn't consent — they're taking care of a daughter who doesn't fully exist, the one without a two-year relationship.

So tell me honestly: in your gut, do you already know you're not going through with Sunday? Or is part of you wondering if you could sit through it just once? I won't judge either answer — I just want to know where we're actually planning from.

Every post I read online says the same thing — "you're 27, it's your life, just tell them clearly: my life, my choice." Part of me wants to just say exactly that at dinner tonight and stop this whole circus before Sunday. Should I? At least everything would finally be out.

I understand the pull — five days of dread compressed into one loud sentence, and it's over. But can I be honest? "My life, my choice" is the right *principle* and probably the worst *script* for your particular dinner table.

That line comes from a framework where individuality is the trump card. In your house, it won't land as truth — it'll land as rejection. Appa will hear "your love means nothing to me." Amma will hear "she's become someone else." And then the conversation is about your *defiance*, not about the man you love. You'll have told them everything and somehow told them nothing.

So yes — talk before Sunday. But not as a declaration of independence. As an invitation *in*:

"Amma, Appa, I need to tell you something, and I'm telling you because I don't want to lie to you. There's someone. Two years. He's a good man, he's serious, and I want you to know him before you decide anything about him."

See the difference? You're not saying "my choice, deal with it." You're saying "I want you in this." It gives them a role other than opponent. Keep caste out of the opening line — let them ask, answer honestly when they do, but don't hand them the ending before the story.

Also, practically: not tonight in a flash of courage-panic. Pick a calm moment tomorrow, maybe Appa first if he's the steadier one, or whichever parent softens the other. And tell your partner today so you're not doing this alone in your head.

One more thing — expect it to go badly *in the moment*. Tears, BP, silence. That's the first reaction, not the final verdict. Families like ours often need weeks to travel what a Reddit post expects in one dinner.

Do you know which parent you'd approach first?

And if they say no in the end — like a real, final no — I honestly don't think I can walk out against them. I've imagined it and I can't. Does that make me weak? Sometimes I think I don't love him enough, then I think I don't love myself enough, and I'm just going in circles at 2am.

No. It doesn't make you weak, and it doesn't mean you don't love him enough. Please hear that.

The "if you really loved him you'd walk out" idea comes from movies where love is proven by burning bridges. But you weren't raised as an individual with a family attached — you were raised as a thread in a fabric. Tearing yourself out of that isn't one brave decision; it's losing your mother's kitchen, your father's voice, weddings, festivals, the whole architecture of who you are. Dreading that isn't weakness. It's knowing what things cost.

And at 2am, your brain is running the worst-case ending of a story that hasn't even started. You're grieving a "final no" that hasn't been said. Most families like ours don't give one clean final no — they give anger, then silence, then negotiation, then a grudging meeting, then, often, slow acceptance. Especially when the daughter stays steady and *doesn't* leave. Your unwillingness to walk out might actually be your leverage: "I'm not choosing between you and him. I'm choosing both. I'll wait for you."

But I'll be honest about the one hard thing: not being able to walk out can't quietly become *walking into the Dallas marriage*. Those aren't the only two doors. There's a third — telling the truth, refusing Sunday, and then patiently, stubbornly staying in your family's life while they come around. That path takes months, not one dramatic night. It suits who you are.

The real question isn't "can I leave my parents?" It's "can I live a whole life with a man I don't love, keeping a secret grief?" You already know that answer — it's why you're awake at 2am.

Have you told him yet how scared you are? He should be carrying some of this with you this week.
